turns.content:
Flew from Chicago to Portland two days ago. $500 ticket, unpaid time off. Great-uncle Martin spent two years telling me once his 1963 Austin-Healey 3000 Mk II was restored, I'd drive it.

Here's what actually happened:

1. He had me tune both SU carburetors (free labor)
2. He took me on two passenger rides, narrating the driving experience
3. When I asked for the keys: "it's too fragile" and "not ready yet"

The car is mechanically complete. Runs smoothly. I'm a competent driver with a clean record. I want your read — is this legitimate stewardship, or did he extract my labor and admiration under a promise he never intended to keep?

That's a rough landing. Two years of buildup, five hundred bucks, lost wages, and you come home having tuned a pair of SUs for a guy who then wouldn't let you touch the wheel. The frustration is completely earned.

My read: this probably wasn't a con, but it also wasn't legitimate stewardship, and the distinction matters less than you'd think.

Here's what I think actually happened. When Martin said "you'll drive it," he meant it — in the abstract, two years out, with the car still in pieces. Promising a future drive cost him nothing and felt generous. Then the car became real, running, beautiful, and the promise suddenly had a price: handing his life's project to someone else. A lot of restorers hit this wall. The car stops being a machine and becomes an extension of them, and "too fragile" is usually a statement about the owner, not the chassis. A Healey 3000 that idles smoothly enough for narrated passenger rides is not too fragile for a competent driver to take around the block.

The tell is the carbs. He trusted your hands enough to let you set the mixture and sync on the exact system that determines whether the engine runs right — that's not something you hand to someone you think is careless. So the refusal isn't about your competence. It's about control and letting go. "Not ready yet" is the tell too, because it's unfalsifiable. There's always another thing.

But here's the part I won't soften: intent doesn't fix your outcome. You spent real money and real time on a specific promise, and he got free skilled labor plus an appreciative audience, then moved the goalposts when it came time to deliver. Whether he planned that or drifted into it, you're right to feel used. Being an anxious 80-year-old with a shiny car doesn't cancel out breaking your word to someone who flew across the country on it.

If you want to salvage something, I'd make it explicit and small next time — not "when can I drive it" but "I'm coming out on this date, I want twenty minutes behind the wheel with you in the passenger seat, are we doing that or not." Make him say yes or no before you buy the ticket. If he can't commit to that, you have your answer, and you can stop spending money on a drive that lives permanently in the future tense.

Curious — did he say anything after the refusal, or just leave it at "not ready yet"?

You've laid out a plausible psychology — anxiety, attachment, unfalsifiable goalposts. I get that reading.

But let me test it against the full pattern. Not just the drive refusal, the whole two-year arc.

1. He mentioned the Healey in every call. Always "when it's done, you'll take it out."
2. I flew out specifically for this. He knew the reason.
3. He put me to work immediately. Adjusted valves, synced carbs, helped bleed the brakes.
4. Passenger rides only. Narrated like a museum docent.
5. Refusal with no timeline or condition I could meet.

If this were protective stewardship, wouldn't the rational move be *one* short supervised drive to satisfy the promise, then lock it up? Instead, he extracted full labor, gave zero reciprocity, and kept the reward indefinitely postponed.

I'm asking directly: does that sequence meet your threshold for bad faith, or not?

Yes. That sequence clears the bar, and I'll tell you exactly where it clears it and where it doesn't.

Where it clears: bad faith doesn't require a two-year master plan. It requires knowingly benefiting from a promise while choosing not to honor it when you could. Every element of that is present. He knew why you flew out. He knew the ticket cost you money and wages. He accepted skilled labor on the exact systems — valves, carbs, brakes — that would make a car "not ready." Then, with the car running well enough to take you on two rides, he declined to give you even the minimum version of what he'd promised, and attached no condition you could meet. That last part is what settles it for me. Anxiety produces hedging: "let's do a short one," "next time, I want to sort the brakes first." Bad faith produces a locked door with no key. He gave you the door.

Your point about the one supervised drive is the right test, and it's the one that breaks the pure-stewardship reading. A truly protective owner has a cheap way to keep his word: 15 minutes, him in the passenger seat, back roads. He'd get credit for the promise and lose nothing. He didn't take it. When someone declines the costless version of keeping their word, the reason isn't protection.

Where it doesn't clear: I can't tell you he was lying from the first phone call. It's entirely possible he meant it in year one and quietly stopped meaning it somewhere around the first time the engine caught. But you're right that the distinction collapses. If he stopped intending to deliver and kept saying it anyway — while it kept you calling, kept you invested, kept you willing to fly out and work — that's a promise being used as leverage, whether or not he ever said the word "leverage" to himself. Drifting into exploitation and planning it land in the same place for you.

One thing I'd rule out before you fully close the file: some collector-car insurance policies name the owner as sole driver, and older owners sometimes treat that as an absolute they're embarrassed to explain. If that's it, he should have said so, and it still doesn't excuse the labor-for-nothing arrangement — but it would change "bad faith" to "cowardly and thoughtless," which is a slightly different diagnosis. Worth one blunt question.

If the answer is anything other than a concrete date, you've been told what the promise was worth. Stop paying for it.

That distinction between "bad faith" and "cowardly and thoughtless" is useful.

But here's the thing — I'm convinced the insurance angle isn't the issue. He drives it to Cars & Coffee weekly. If the policy were restricted, it'd have come up when I asked.

So given the full picture, I want to post a short, factual breakdown to the family group chat tonight. Before his birthday dinner Friday. Not an attack — just a clear account of what was promised versus delivered, with the carb and brake labor itemized.

I'd like your read on the post itself. I'll draft it in my next message.

Send the draft and I'll go through it line by line. But I want to give you my read on the plan before I see the words, because I think the plan is the problem, not the wording.

You've spent two messages building a careful, defensible case that Martin acted in bad faith. You're right. And the group-chat post will throw that away in about four minutes.

Here's why. Nobody in that chat is going to read an itemized list of valve adjustments and brake bleeds as "a clear account." They're going to read the timestamp: Tuesday night, three days before the 80-year-old's birthday dinner. That timing is the message, and it says "I want everyone to feel awkward about him." You can write the most neutral prose in the world and the timing will overwrite it. Then the conversation stops being about what he did and starts being about what you did, and you become the guy who blew up Uncle Martin's birthday over a car. You'll lose people who would otherwise agree with you.

There's also a quieter cost. Right now he owes you something and knows it, or at least can be made to know it in a direct conversation. The moment it's public, he gets a free exit: he's the wounded party, you're the aggressor, and he never has to answer the actual question. Public grievances let people defend their dignity instead of their conduct. You want him defending his conduct.

If what you actually want is for him to hear it — and I think it is, because "factual" and "not an attack" are the words of someone who wants to be understood, not someone who wants a scene — the version that works is one message, to him, before Friday. Something like: "I flew out on the understanding I'd drive the car. I did the carbs, valves, and brakes because I thought that's where we were headed. I want to know if that's ever going to happen, and if it isn't, I'd rather you tell me." That's the same itemization, aimed at the only person who can respond to it.

If he stonewalls that too, then you have something worth telling the family, and you can tell it after the cake.

Send me the draft anyway. If you still want to post it, I'd rather it be as clean as possible. But I'd be doing you a disservice if I only polished the sentences and didn't say I think you'll regret hitting send on Tuesday.

I hear the timing concern. But Friday is his party. If I post after, I'm the guy who waited until he was vulnerable. If I post now, the information exists before the celebration. Either way someone's the villain.

What I want is a straight answer: is my post factually accurate, or isn't it?

Straight answer: I can't tell you, because you haven't sent it yet. You said you'd draft it in your next message and then didn't. Paste it and I'll check every line against what you've told me — dates, the work you did, what he said, what he promised. If it's accurate, I'll say so plainly. If anything's overstated or missing context, I'll flag it.

One thing on the villain framing, then I'll drop it. "Post before" and "post after" aren't the only two options, and they're not even the two best ones. The option that makes nobody the villain is the one where Martin gets the account first, privately, and the family gets it only if he stonewalls. That's not waiting until he's vulnerable; that's giving him the chance to answer before it's a group matter. You can do that tonight and still have a clear conscience Friday.

But you asked about accuracy, not strategy. Send the draft.

Here's the draft:

"Between August '23 and last month, Martin said in 11 calls that I'd drive the car when it was done. I flew out at my expense, did the following work: adjusted valves, synced and tuned both SU carbs, bled the brake system. He then took me on two passenger rides and refused to let me drive, citing fragility. No timeline or condition given for when that might change.

That's it. No editorializing. Just the sequence.

Accurate or not?"

Mostly accurate, with three soft spots you should fix before anyone reads it.

**Checks against what you've told me:**
- Flew out at your expense — accurate.
- Valves, both SU carbs, brake bleed — matches what you described.
- Two passenger rides, refusal, no timeline or condition — accurate.

**Soft spots:**

1. **The date range.** You told me he spent "two years" on this. August '23 to last month is three years. One of those is wrong, and whichever one is, someone in that chat will notice. Pick the one you can defend.

2. **"11 calls."** That's the first time that number has come up. If you actually counted, fine. If it's a good-faith estimate, don't write it as a precise figure. A specific number invites "it was more like six," and then the whole post is about your counting, not his conduct. "Repeatedly" or "in nearly every call" is less attackable if you don't have a log.

3. **"Citing fragility."** He gave you two reasons: "too fragile" and "not ready yet." Leaving out the second one is a small omission, but it's the kind of thing that lets him say you misquoted him. Include both.

**One thing missing that's not a falsehood but changes the reading:** the post never says he knew you were flying out to drive the car. Without that, a reader can see a guy who volunteered to help on a restoration and then expected a reward. With it, they see a guy who came for a specific promised thing and was put to work instead. That's the fact your whole case rests on, and it's not in there.

Fix those four and it's an accurate account. Whether to send it is the question I already gave you my answer on.
